Refractive index is a property of the **two media and the light**, not of how the ray
happens to strike the surface.
**Step 1 — state Snell's law.**
n₂₁ = sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ ✓
The **ratio** sin i/sin r is the same for every angle of incidence - that is the content
of the law, and it means the refractive index is **independent of the angle** ✓ So the
fourth statement is the **incorrect** one.
**Step 2 — check the other three.**
"**depends on the nature of the first medium**" ✓ **true** - n₂₁ = v₁/v₂, and v₁ belongs
to the first medium.
"**depends on the nature of the second medium**" ✓ **true** - for the same reason.
"**depends on the wavelength of light**" ✓ **true** - this is **dispersion**; violet
light is refracted more than red, which is why a prism makes a spectrum.
**How the wavelength dependence shows itself.** For crown glass,
violet (400 nm): n = **1·53**
red (700 nm): n = **1·51** ✓
a small difference, but enough to spread sunlight into a rainbow, and enough to cause
chromatic aberration in lenses.
**Cauchy's formula.** n = A + B/λ² ✓ so n **falls** as the wavelength grows - normal
dispersion, obeyed by all transparent materials away from absorption bands.
**Why the angle independence is remarkable.** It was not obvious before Snell: Ptolemy
had tabulated i against r and found no simple rule, because he compared the **angles**
rather than their **sines** ✓ The constancy of sin i/sin r is exactly what makes a
refractive index a meaningful material constant.
**The one apparent exception.** At the **critical angle** and beyond, there is no
refracted ray at all ✓ But that is total internal reflection, not a change in n - the
index is unchanged, and sin r would simply exceed 1.
**What n does also depend on.** Temperature and pressure, slightly, through the
density ✓ and on the **direction** of propagation in a birefringent crystal such as
calcite - but never on the angle of incidence for a given pair of isotropic media.
∴ it depends upon angle of incidence.

The rotation measures the **concentration of sugar actually present**; compare it with
the total concentration of the sample.
**Step 1 — state the polarimeter relation.**
θ = S l c ✓
with θ the optical rotation, S the specific rotation, l the tube length and c the
concentration of the **active** substance.
**Step 2 — solve for the sugar concentration.**
c = θ/(S l)
= 0·4/(0·01 x 0·25)
= 0·4/0·0025
= **160 kg m⁻³** ✓
**Step 3 — compare with the total concentration.** The solution contains 200 kg m⁻³ of
**impure** sugar, of which only 160 kg m⁻³ is actually sugar:
purity = 160/200
= 0·80
= **80%** ✓
**Why the impurity does not rotate.** Only **optically active** substances rotate the
plane of polarisation ✓ The inactive impurity contributes to the mass but not to the
rotation - which is precisely what makes the measurement a purity test.
**Why sugar is optically active.** Its molecules are **chiral** - they exist in
left- and right-handed forms that are mirror images ✓ Natural sucrose is
dextrorotatory, turning the plane clockwise, which is why it is called **dextrose** in
some contexts.
**Where this is used commercially.** Sugar refineries and customs laboratories measure
purity exactly this way ✓ The instrument is called a **saccharimeter**, and the
specific rotation of sucrose is a standard reference value.
**A check on the units.**
[θ] = [S][l][c] = (SI units)(m)(kg m⁻³) ✓ so S must have units of rad m² kg⁻¹, which is
what "0·01 SI units" means. The arithmetic is consistent.
**Why the tube length matters.** A longer tube means more molecules in the path and a
larger rotation ✓ Precision polarimeters use long tubes for dilute solutions.
**Reading the distractors.** **89%** ✗, **11%** ✗ and **20%** ✗ correspond to
concentrations of 178, 22 and 40 kg m⁻³, none of which satisfies θ = Slc ✓ Note that
20% is the **impurity**, not the purity - a trap for the hurried.
∴ 80%.

In circular motion the centripetal force points **along the radius** while the motion is
**along the tangent** - so the two are perpendicular and no work is done.
**Step 1 — recall the definition of work.**
W = F̄·d̄s̄ = F ds **cos θ** ✓
**Step 2 — find the angle.** The centripetal force points towards the **centre**; the
displacement at each instant is along the **tangent** ✓ A radius and the tangent at the
same point meet at a right angle, so **θ = 90°**.
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
W = F ds cos 90°
= **0** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** No work is done because the force and displacement are
**perpendicular** ✓
**The energy check.** For **uniform** circular motion the speed, and hence the kinetic
energy, is constant ✓ By the work-energy theorem W = ΔKE = 0 - exactly consistent.
**Why the other explanations fail.**
"**there is no displacement**" ✗ - the body plainly moves; after a full circle the
**net** displacement is zero, but over any short interval it is not, and the
instantaneous work is zero at every instant, not merely over a whole lap.
"**there is no net force**" ✗ - there certainly is: mv²/r, directed inward. Without it
the body would fly off along the tangent.
"**the force is always away from the centre**" ✗ - the centripetal force points
**towards** the centre; and even if it pointed outward it would still do no work ✓
**Everyday examples of workless forces.**
the Earth's gravity on a satellite in a **circular** orbit - which is why the orbit
needs no fuel ✓
the **magnetic** force on a moving charge, always perpendicular to v̄
the **tension** in the string of a whirling stone
the **normal reaction** on a body sliding along a surface ✓
**Why an elliptical orbit is different.** There the force is **not** always
perpendicular to the motion, so work **is** done, and the satellite speeds up near
perihelion and slows near aphelion ✓ The total energy remains constant, but kinetic and
potential energy are exchanged.
∴ force and displacement are perpendicular to each other.

The speed of sound in a gas goes as **1/√M**, so the lighter gas carries sound faster.
**Step 1 — write the speed.**
v = √(γRT/M) ✓
**Step 2 — note what is common.** Both gases are **diatomic**, so γ = 1·4 for each, and
both are at STP, so T is the same ✓ Only the molar mass differs.
**Step 3 — form the ratio.**
v_H/v_O = √(M_O/M_H)
= √(32/2)
= √16
= **4 : 1** ✓
**The actual speeds at STP.**
in hydrogen: **1270 m s⁻¹** ✓
in oxygen: **317 m s⁻¹**
and their ratio is **4·0** ✓ as calculated.
**Why the lighter gas is faster.** Sound travels by molecular collisions, and lighter
molecules move faster at the same temperature ✓ Their mean speed goes as 1/√M, and the
sound speed follows the same law.
**The famous demonstration.** Inhale helium and the voice rises in pitch ✓ The vocal
tract's resonant frequencies go as the sound speed, and helium (M = 4) carries sound
nearly three times faster than air (M = 29). The **pitch of the vocal cords** does not
change; the resonances do.
**Why γ matters too.** Comparing hydrogen with a **monatomic** gas such as helium would
need the γ values as well ✓ Here both gases are diatomic, so γ cancels - a point worth
checking before using the simple √(M₂/M₁).
**The temperature dependence.** v ∝ √T ✓ so sound in air travels at 331 m s⁻¹ at 0 °C
and about 343 m s⁻¹ at 20 °C - which is why the speed is always quoted with a
temperature.
**What sound speed does not depend on.** The **pressure**, at constant temperature ✓
since P and ρ rise together in P/ρ = RT/M. Sound travels at the same speed at the top of
a mountain as at sea level, if the temperatures match.
**Reading the distractors.** **16 : 1** ✗ is the **mass** ratio, with the square root
forgotten - the commonest error. **8 : 1** ✗ and **2 : 1** ✗ match no power of 16 ✓
∴ 4 : 1.

Two Doppler equations for a **moving observer**; divide them to eliminate the source
frequency.
**Step 1 — write the approaching case.**
f₁ = f(v + v_o)/v = **200 Hz** ✓
**Step 2 — write the receding case.**
f₂ = f(v − v_o)/v = **160 Hz** ✓
**Step 3 — divide.**
(v + v_o)/(v − v_o) = 200/160
= **5/4**
**Step 4 — cross-multiply with v_o = 40.**
4(v + 40) = 5(v − 40)
4v + 160 = 5v − 200
**v = 360 m s⁻¹** ✓
**Step 5 — find the source frequency, as a check.**
f = f₁ v/(v + v_o)
= 200(360)/400
= **180 Hz** ✓
and the receding case: 180(320)/360 = **160 Hz** ✓ exactly as given.
**Why the observer's formula has v_o in the numerator.** A moving observer changes the
**rate at which wavefronts arrive**, not their spacing ✓ The wavelength in the air is
unaltered; only the relative speed of approach changes, from v to v + v_o.
**The contrast with a moving source.** There the **wavelength itself** is compressed
ahead of the source, and v_s appears in the **denominator**:
f′ = fv/(v − v_s) ✓
The two cases give different answers for the same relative speed - a real physical
distinction, not a bookkeeping one, because the medium singles out a preferred frame.
**A neat check on the arithmetic.** The **average** of the two apparent frequencies,
(200 + 160)/2 = **180 Hz**, is exactly the true frequency ✓ This always holds for a
moving observer, because the two shifts are symmetric: f(1 ± v_o/v).
**Why 360 m s⁻¹ rather than the usual 340.** The question's numbers fix it; 360 m s⁻¹
corresponds to air at about **49 °C** ✓ warm, but physically possible.
**Reading the distractors.** **340** ✗ would give apparent frequencies in the ratio
380/300 = 1·27, not 1·25. **330** ✗ and **320** ✗ are further off ✓ Substituting each
into (v + 40)/(v − 40) and comparing with 1·25 tests them at once.
∴ 360.

The radius of a charged particle's circular path is **r = mv/(qB)**, so track what
happens to v and B.
**Step 1 — write the radius.** The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force:
qvB = mv²/r
**r = mv/(qB)** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the two changes.**
speed **doubled**: v → 2v, so r is multiplied by **2**
field **halved**: B → B/2, so r is multiplied by **2** ✓
**Step 3 — combine.**
r′ = r x 2 x 2
= **4r** ✓
**Why both changes push the same way.** A faster particle is harder to bend, and a
weaker field bends it less ✓ Neither effect opposes the other, so the radius grows
fourfold.
**What does not change - the sense of the motion.** The particle still circles in the
same direction, since neither the sign of the charge nor the direction of B has
altered ✓
**What does change - the period.**
T = 2πm/(qB) ✓
This is **independent of the speed**, a remarkable fact, but it does depend on B.
Halving B **doubles** the period, so the slower circulation is entirely due to the
weaker field.
**Why the speed-independence of T matters.** It is the principle of the **cyclotron** ✓
Particles of every energy take the same time per revolution, so a fixed-frequency
alternating voltage can accelerate them turn after turn - at least until relativistic
mass increase spoils it.
**A worked instance.** An electron at 10⁶ m s⁻¹ in 0·01 T:
r = (9·1 x 10⁻³¹)(10⁶)/[(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹)(0·01)] = **5·7 x 10⁻⁴ m**
double v and halve B: r = **2·3 x 10⁻³ m** ✓ four times larger.
**The quantity r measures.** For given q and B, r is proportional to the **momentum**
mv ✓ which is why magnetic spectrometers measure particle momenta by measuring radii of
curvature in bubble-chamber photographs.
**Reading the distractors.** **2r** ✗ accounts for only one of the two changes. **r/2**
✗ and **r** ✗ have the radius shrinking or unchanged, though both changes enlarge it ✓
∴ 4 r.

For the electron to go **straight**, the electric and magnetic forces must balance -
the velocity-selector condition.
**Step 1 — write the balance.**
qE = qvB
**v = E/B** ✓ the charge cancelling, so the result holds for any charged particle.
**Step 2 — substitute.**
v = 1500/0·40
= **3750 m s⁻¹**
= **3·75 x 10³ m s⁻¹** ✓
**Why the fields must be mutually perpendicular.** Only then do the two forces act along
the **same line** and cancel ✓ The electron's velocity must be perpendicular to both,
which is the standard crossed-field arrangement.
**Why this speed is "minimum" or unique.** At exactly v = E/B the forces balance and the
path is straight ✓ Faster, and the magnetic force wins, curving the electron one way;
slower, and the electric force wins, curving it the other. Only one speed passes
undeflected.
**Why the charge and mass are irrelevant.** Both forces carry the factor q, which
cancels ✓ A proton, an alpha particle or an electron at 3750 m s⁻¹ would all pass
straight through - the device selects **speed**, not particle type.
**Where this is used.** As the **velocity selector** stage of a mass spectrometer ✓ A
beam of mixed speeds enters, and only those at E/B emerge through the exit slit. A
second magnetic field then separates them by m/q through r = mv/(qB), with v now known.
**Its historical importance.** J. J. Thomson used crossed fields in 1897 to measure
**e/m** for the electron ✓ balancing the fields to find v, then removing the electric
field and measuring the deflection to get e/m - the experiment that discovered the
electron.
**Checking the units.**
[E/B] = (V m⁻¹)/(T) = (V m⁻¹)/(V s m⁻²) = **m s⁻¹** ✓ a speed, as required.
**Reading the distractors.** **1·6 x 10¹⁵ m s⁻¹** ✗ exceeds the speed of light - an
impossible answer, and worth spotting at once. **6 x 10⁻¹⁶** ✗ is absurdly small, and
**3·75 x 10²** ✗ is a factor of ten out ✓
∴ 3.75 × 10³ m/s.

An inertial frame is one moving at **constant velocity** - no acceleration of any kind.
**Step 1 — state the test.** A frame is inertial if it has **zero acceleration**, so
that a free body in it stays at rest or moves in a straight line at constant speed ✓
Any acceleration - speeding up, slowing down, or **turning** - makes the frame
non-inertial.
**Step 2 — examine each case.**
**a child on a giant wheel** ✗ - moving in a circle, so continuously accelerating
towards the centre. **Non-inertial.**
**a driver at constant 200 km/h on a straight road** ✓ - constant speed **and** constant
direction, so zero acceleration. **Inertial.**
**the pilot of an aeroplane taking off** ✗ - accelerating along the runway and then
climbing. **Non-inertial.**
**a cyclist negotiating a sharp curve** ✗ - centripetal acceleration again.
**Non-inertial.**
**Step 3 — conclude.** Only the driver on the straight road is in an inertial frame ✓
**Why high speed does not matter.** 200 km/h is fast, but **speed** is irrelevant ✓ Only
**changes** in velocity matter. A passenger in a smoothly cruising aircraft can pour a
drink exactly as on the ground.
**Why turning counts as acceleration.** Velocity is a **vector** ✓ Changing its
direction changes it, even at constant speed - which is why both the giant wheel and the
curve are non-inertial.
**The qualification "for ordinary terrestrial experiments".** The Earth itself rotates
and orbits the Sun, so a frame fixed to the ground is **strictly** non-inertial ✓ But
the centripetal acceleration at the equator is only **0·034 m s⁻²**, about 0·3% of g,
so for everyday purposes the ground - and anything moving uniformly with respect to it -
counts as inertial.
**Where the Earth's rotation does show.** In the **Coriolis** deflection of winds and
ocean currents, in the slow turning of a **Foucault pendulum**, and in the drift of
long-range projectiles ✓ All are evidence that the ground frame is not quite inertial.
∴ a driver in a sports car moving with a constant high speed of 200 kmh⁻¹ on a straight
road.

At the polarising angle, **n = tan i_p**; then the speed in the medium follows from
v = c/n.
**Step 1 — apply Brewster's law.**
n = tan i_p
= tan 60°
= **√3** ✓
**Step 2 — find the speed of light in the glass.**
v = c/n
= 3 x 10⁸/√3
= **√3 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** ✓
since 3/√3 = √3.
**Step 3 — evaluate.** √3 x 10⁸ = **1·73 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** ✓ a little over half the speed in
vacuum, as a refractive index of 1·73 requires.
**Why Brewster's law takes that form.** At the polarising angle the reflected and
refracted rays are **perpendicular**, so i_p + r = 90° ✓ Then
n = sin i_p/sin r = sin i_p/cos i_p = **tan i_p** ✓
**What is special about the reflected light there.** It is **completely plane-polarised**,
with its electric field perpendicular to the plane of incidence ✓ The refracted ray is
only partially polarised.
**Why the reflection loses one polarisation.** The refracted ray sets the medium's
electrons oscillating along its own direction, and a dipole cannot radiate along its
own axis ✓ At Brewster's angle that axis points exactly where the reflected ray would
go, so that component is absent.
**A check on the index.** n = √3 = **1·73** is high for ordinary glass (1·5) but
matches a dense flint glass ✓ and gives a critical angle of sin⁻¹(1/1·73) = **35·3°**.
**The everyday use.** Light reflected from water or a road near Brewster's angle is
strongly polarised horizontally ✓ Polarising sunglasses block that component, which is
why they cut glare so effectively.
**Reading the distractors.** **3 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** ✗ is the speed in **vacuum**, which no
medium can match. **2 x 10⁸** ✗ corresponds to n = 1·5, and **√2 x 10⁸** ✗ to
n = √2 ✓ Only tan 60° = √3 fits the given polarising angle.
∴ √3 × 10⁸ ms⁻¹.
